articles.title: The Tejano singer trying to win back Latinos who voted for Trump, one quinceañera at a time
articles.description: Bobby Pulido has a strategy: show up at the 15th birthday parties that are a rite of passage in the Texas borderlands – and flip a key House district for Democrats
articles.body:
Bobby Pulido pictured for the Guardian in September 2026. Photograph: Brenda Bazán/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Bobby Pulido pictured for the Guardian in September 2026. Photograph: Brenda Bazán/The Guardian Texas The Tejano singer trying to win back Latinos who voted for Trump, one quinceañera at a time Bobby Pulido has a strategy: show up at the 15th birthday parties that are a rite of passage in the Texas borderlands – and flip a key House district for Democrats
It took all of two minutes for Bobby Pulido’s electoral stealth weapon to come into play. The Tejano music star turned Democratic congressional candidate had barely begun canvassing in the high school football stadium in Edinburg, Texas , when a 15-year-old girl came rushing up to him.
“Señor Pulido! Señor Pulido!” she cried. A few months ago, she told him, he had made a surprise appearance at her quinceañera, the coming-of-age girls’ 15th birthday party that is a rite of passage in these US borderlands.
He had serenaded her with Desvelado , his blockbuster love song, which though released three decades ago retains a treasured place in Tejano – that is Hispanic Texan – culture.
The brief encounter gave a glimpse into one of the key dynamics of Pulido’s bid to flip Texas’s 15th congressional district. He calls it the “quinceañera strategy”.
The tactic was handed to him, inadvertently, by his rival, the two-term incumbent Republican congresswoman Monica De La Cruz. In March, she posted a video deriding her opponent as a lowly quinceañera singer.
The election, she said, “isn’t about who you want performing at your niece’s quinceañera. It’s about who you trust with your family’s future.”
Pulido pounced. He counter-posted his own video in which he accused De La Cruz of belittling a cherished local tradition and encouraged families in the district planning a quinceañera to invite him. “I’d be honored to stop by and celebrate with you,” he said.
Within 24 hours, Pulido’s campaign had been inundated with over 1,000 invitations. By the time the Guardian went canvassing with him in September, that number had surpassed 5,000.
View image in fullscreen Bobby Pulido visits a high school football game in Edinburg, Texas, last month. He has now performed at 81 quinceañeras and counting. Each one is attended by scores of family and friends, most of whom are eligible voters and many of whom livestream the event on their smartphones, broadcasting it to additional scores of eligible voters.
“She presented us with an opportunity for a very unique kind of field plan,” Abel Prado, Pulido’s campaign manager, said.
Pulido, 53, is hoping to convert the quinceañera strategy and the rest of the tireless retail politics that he is doing into a winning political formula. His mission: to take back the congressional seat, and in the process both help the national Democratic party regain control of the US House and teach it a lesson or two about Mexican American politics.
It’s not just that flipping Texas 15 could give Democrats the edge they need to take back control of the House of Representatives. The stakes are also huge for the Rio Grande Valley itself, the overwhelmingly Hispanic border region in south Texas that for over a century was solidly Democratic but swung hard for Donald Trump in 2024.
Trump won the district, which is 81% Mexican American and which runs for over 300 miles from the border to San Antonio, by 18 points.
How Pulido fares in the November midterm elections could have ripple effects for fellow Democrat James Talarico’s currently neck-and-neck fight for a US Senate seat against the state’s scandal-ridden Republican attorney general Ken Paxton. Talarico’s chance of success is also heavily dependent on Latino turnout.
And in the widest sense, Pulido’s message has bearings on the national Democratic party as it debates how to counter the dramatic inroads made by Trump two years ago when he smashed records and garnered 55% of Texas’s Hispanic vote.
Pulido made sure to display his Tejano stripes as he strutted around the Edinburg stadium, while cheerleaders and a marching band filled the night air with colour and noise. Dressed in jeans and denim shirt, cowboy boots and hat, he moved confidently through the crowd of high-school football fans.
He shook the hand of everyone he met, chatting to supporters on both sides of the bleachers – a calculated move as both high school teams, Sabrecats and Yellowjackets, are in the 15th district. (The Sabrecats won 31-14.)
And yet almost everyone in attendance was too young to vote – so what was the point?
“To win re-election,” Pulido quipped, without missing a beat. Then, with more reflection, he added: “If you treat kids good, their parents will like you.”
Pulido has a catchphrase : “Any occasion, big or small.” He means it. The football game was the 526th campaign event he had attended in person. His record is 12 such stops in a single day.
View image in fullscreen Pulido greets the mother of the cheerleading coach via video call at the football game. When Pulido sat down to talk with the Guardian, he emphasised accessibility was a critical element of his campaign. It’s his answer, he said, to the increasingly polarised left-right media bubbles that keep voters divided.
“The only way I can break through is to actually get in front of people the old-fashioned way. Then people can hear me. They can look me in the eye, and decide for themselves whether I’m full of shit or not.”
Direct connection with voters also Pulido, who has roots stretching back seven generations in the Rio Grande Valley, allows him to play his ace card: his near-universal name recognition in the region.
Desvelado (“sleepless”) was his first, and is still his biggest, hit – the 1995 album of the same name went platinum, and the song has been played 615m times on Spotify. He has won two Latin Grammys for best Tejano album; the day before we met he celebrated yet another nomination for the award, for Una Tuya, Una Mía, Vol 2.

articles.title: Saturday Night Live: Dakota Johnson struggles through weak episode as Taylor Swift gatecrashes
articles.description: The Verity star’s awkwardness with live comedy is matched with similarly sub-par writing in an episode featuring a surprise cameo from her superstar friend
articles.body:
Dakota Johnson and Taylor Swift on Saturday Night Live. Photograph: YouTube View image in fullscreen Dakota Johnson and Taylor Swift on Saturday Night Live. Photograph: YouTube Saturday Night Live Saturday Night Live: Dakota Johnson struggles through weak episode as Taylor Swift gatecrashes The Verity star’s awkwardness with live comedy is matched with similarly sub-par writing in an episode featuring a surprise cameo from her superstar friend
Prefer the Guardian on Google S aturday Night Live kicks off the second episode of its new season at RNC headquarters. With the midterms looking bleak for Republicans, strategists bring out some heavy hitters to record TV ads. Marco Rubio (Marcello Hernández) delivers a message in Spanish putting all of the blame on Trump (“Oh my God! He tricked us!”); a comatose Mitch McConnell (Mikey Day) is rolled in to flash the peace sign; and Vice-President JD Vance (Jeremy Culhane) tries to make his pitch for 2028, only to be laughed out of the room. Secretary of war Pete Hegseth (Colin Jost) barges in, chugging “Spider-Man’s new non-alcoholic bitch beer” to demand voters “do the gayest thing ever and vote”.
Read more Finally, president Trump (James Austin Johnson) interrupts to deliver a rambling diatribe, promising checks for five grand to voters if they re-elect Republicans (“that’s not a bribe because I have no intention to follow through on that promise”), test out some terrible new slogans (“imagination makes a Maga nation”), and record victory and concession messages, both of which are the same: “We did it, we won!”
A much better cold open than last week, if still wanting. The show relied a little too heavily of Jost’s Hegseth last season, but the passage of time makes for a fun return here.
Dakota Johnson hosts for the second time. The actor will celebrate her birthday at the stroke of midnight by doing the same thing she does every year: “Stand in midtown in a tight-ass latex dress looking for attention.” She devotes most of her monologue making self-deprecating jokes about her high-profile failed relationships with musicians, before her BFF Taylor Swift joins her on stage, playing reluctant therapist to the romantically-challenged star. Swift’s entrance gets a huge pop from the studio audience, but the jokes elicit little more than chuckles.
Then, Johnson plays Elizabeth Banks, host of the game show Press Your Luck. Players spin a digital wheel for prizes, trying to avoid little red trouble maker The Whammy, who erases their points. Overexcited contestant Sherri (Ashley Padilla) immediately scores the million dollar prize, but stupidly continues on, only to land on the Whammy and lose it all. The same thing happens again and again, much to the chagrin of Banks and the other contestants. This is all yelling.
Mean Scary Girlfriend is a cruel, icy partner who tells helpless guys the harsh truth, making their lives both easier and way, way more stressful. Not particularly funny, but a good use of Johnson’s sexy ice queen demeanor.
At a hospital cafeteria, a trio of nurses spread work gossip until they’re interrupted by nerdy Eric from legal (Culhane), who uses the dish sesh to reveal sad information about himself (“I heard Eric from legal has an AI girlfriend – had, she killed herself”). The premise is promising, but it goes nowhere and quickly sputters out.
This is followed by a commercial for the Glunt, the first “gun for women”. It’s a pink sidearm in the shape of a vagina, with a “hard to find” trigger and available “at the opposite of Dick’s Sporting Goods”. This one is over and done with before you even realize it.
On a new Game of Thrones spin-off, Johnson and Ben Marshall play members of the royal court, whose attempts to get it on “brother-style” are continually interrupted by her fire breathing dragon, who remains in their bed chamber and likes to watch. There’s some impressive animatronics on display, but every joke falls completely flat.
Indie rockers Turnstile bring some much needed energy to the show with their first set of the night, then its on to Weekend Update. Michael Che and Jost take a page from classic Late Night with Conan O’Brian’s playbook, touching on the Cornell rape case by way of Che solemnly chastising men who don’t hold predators accountable while the camera tellingly lingers on a guilty-looking Jost.
The segment’s first guests are Jason and Link, the protagonists of the highly-anticipated new Grand Theft Auto and Zelda video games, respectively. The former promises “destruction, chaos, and sex”, while the latter boasts “TMPNG: too many puzzles, no guns.” Day follows up his show-stealing performance last week with another bombastic turn as the dweeby Link, getting his fellow cast members to break at just about every line.
Featured player Kam Patterson pretends to be a proud “Gleek”, ecstatic over the news that Glee is coming back to TV, before Che tells him, “You don’t have to say yes to every idea the white writers pitch to you.”
Then, Che welcomes on Debbie the Matchmaker (Sarah Sherman), who tries to set him up with other hopeless singles, including a phonebook’s worth of ex-felons, author and transphobe JK Rowling, a ghost, Mrs Potato Head, “the girl who crapped her pants during the Chinese marathon”, and, finally, herself. Sherman is at her bizarre best here, and its fun to see her playing off/tormenting Che instead of Jost for a change, although it feels like a missed opportunity to not include Johnson, considering she recently played a matchmaker in the popular film Materialists.
At a middle school girl sleepover, three tweens watch a series of get ready with me videos on TikTok. They land on Colorado Vicky, an unwell influencer who shares insane beauty tips while getting 51/50’d and performing self-lobotomies. Just as unwell is the host girl’s dead-eyed, suicidal father (“he’s just in a funk because mom left, his boss found his Sailor Moon costume, and he just found out Draft Kings is real money”). articles.title: Manhattan ‘mole’ mystery: rumors of lost gold spur clandestine excursions into New York sewers
articles.description: A recent arrest suggests that underground invaders of city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuables
articles.body:
Reports of mysterious gangs of sewer spelunkers have transfixed New Yorkers over the summer. Photograph: william87/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Reports of mysterious gangs of sewer spelunkers have transfixed New Yorkers over the summer. Photograph: william87/Getty Images New York Manhattan ‘mole’ mystery: rumors of lost gold spur clandestine excursions into New York sewers A recent arrest suggests that underground invaders of city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuables
Adam Gabbatt in New York Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T here’s been one thing in particular that has been intriguing New Yorkers this summer: the existence, and whereabouts, of so-called “ mole people ” – a mysterious group of individuals who spend at least some of their time wading about in the city’s sewers.
New Yorkers learned a bit more about the phenomenon this week, when two men were caught red – or perhaps another color – handed, after allegedly emerging from a tunnel in Manhattan. Their arrests have shed some light on a slew of instances where people have been witnessed lifting manhole covers and clambering underground.
Samuel Reveron and Kevin Rodriguez were apprehended in Queens after police tracked them down through video footage. The pair were allegedly spotted entering the sewers with four other people, who have yet to be identified.
Read more Both were charged with criminal trespassing, but it is the reason the men gave for their adventure that has proved particularly fascinating.
“We go into the sewer and look for valuables that get stuck in the storm drains and sewers, gold, anything of value,” Reveron, 25, reportedly told police after his arrest.
The gang’s quest fits an apparently misguided pattern of people thinking New York’s sewers are paved with gold. Last year, three men were arrested after they were allegedly seen emerging from a sewer in Brooklyn, one of them telling police : “The reason we went down there is that people lose their gold down there. We got to get it and sell it to make money.”
Despite that vaulting ambition, there is little evidence that sewer foraging is a lucrative trade. Steve Duncan, a former urban explorer who has spent a lot of time in New York’s sewers and subway tunnels, told the New York Times that in more than 100 sewer trips, the most valuable thing he found was an expired credit card.
Still, the penchant for sewer exploration continues. In May this year there were three separate reported incidents of people climbing down into sewers, two of which were captured on video . In footage of the first incident, three people, wearing dungaree-style hip waders and carrying flashlights, walk into the middle of the road in Astoria, Queens. They haul a circular man cover aside, and descend into the darkness of the sewer.
“Three random guys walking around in a strange suit. Open the sewer, go in like the Ninja Turtles,” eyewitness Aki Jakupovic told NBC New York at the time.
Jakupovic isn’t the first to make the comparison to the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a fictional group of human-turtle hybrids who, across a comic book, cartoon TV show and feature film, are depicted as living in the sewers. Per canon, the turtles mutated into humanoids after being exposed to a toxic green goo. They are subsequently trained in martial arts by a large rat.
The turtles, who are brothers, fight crime, frequently crossing paths with a man called Shredder and his accomplices Bebop, who is a mutant warthog, and Rocksteady, who is a sort of rhino. They also encounter Krang, an alien blob-thing who lives in a robot.
While there appears to have been an increase in sewer incidents this year, this isn’t a new phenomenon. In 2015, a trainee at the New York department of environmental protection was arrested after being caught in the sewers, and last year three men were arrested after entering the sewer system in Brooklyn, allegedly in an attempt to find gold.
“God knows what they were looking for. I know for damn sure I wouldn’t be crawling through the sewers of New York, but these three were evidently looking for something,” the then New York police commissioner, Bill Bratton, told journalists at the time.
Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US
Reveron and Rodriguez’s September sojourn might have been written off as a bit of a hoot, but police were seemingly extra interested because it coincided with world leaders gathering at the UN, some of them staying at swanky hotels close to where the two men went underground.
Brian Kennedy, an attorney for Reveron, dismissed those concerns when he spoke to NBC News .
“It seems like not much of a case,” Kennedy told NBC News. “I understand that it is strange that it’s alleged he went [into the sewer]. But there’s no connection to the UN or the appearance of Netanyahu or any other kind of nefarious scheme.”
It’s both strange and dangerous, Rob Wolejsza, a spokesperson for New York’s department of environmental protection, previously told the Guardian . Wolejsza said it was “both illegal and extremely dangerous” to go into the sewers, adding: “Sewers can contain numerous hazards, including noxious and potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces, flooding risks and confined spaces. For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole or outfall.”
Whether people will listen remains to be seen. On the same day Reveron and Rodriguez were arrested, another three men were spotted climbing out of a sewer at 4.30am in Bensonhurst, south Brooklyn.
ABC7NY reported that police found a shovel in the sewer, but the men got away.

articles.title: Trump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a reality | Steve Bloomfield
articles.description: The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling, says journalist Steve Bloomfield
articles.body:
Flavio Bolsonaro at a rally in Campo Grande, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, 3 October 2026. Photograph: Bruna Prado/AP View image in fullscreen Flavio Bolsonaro at a rally in Campo Grande, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, 3 October 2026. Photograph: Bruna Prado/AP Opinion Brazil Trump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a reality Steve Bloomfield The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling
D onald Trump has enjoyed very few foreign policy victories since returning to power. From failed wars to failed peace processes, his second term in office has been marked by one costly blunder on the world stage after another. In Latin America, though, the US president has a different story to tell.
His administration’s national security strategy outlined how the US wanted to “restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere”. It was a brazen document, laying out how his government would interfere in the political life of countries it considered part of its sphere of influence, rewarding governments and movements that are “broadly aligned with our principles and strategy”.
To this end, Trump bailed out Argentina to the tune of $40bn and threatened to withdraw the funding if President Javier Milei’s party lost the midterm elections. In Colombia, he repeatedly bullied and threatened the leftwing president, Gustavo Petro, hitting him with personal sanctions and accusing him of being an “illegal drug leader”. And most dramatically, he invaded Venezuela and kidnapped its president. The day after Nicolás Maduro was brought to the US, the state department posted a picture of Trump above the slogan “This is OUR hemisphere”.
Over the past 18 months, seven rightwing or far-right candidates have won presidential elections across Latin America. In most of them, Trump openly backed the winning candidate. “We’re doing very well in South America,” Trump said last month. “Lots of people that I got elected.”
This weekend, he will be hoping to add the greatest prize of all: Brazil, South America’s biggest country and its largest economy. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, is neck and neck with the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva . If he wins, Trump wins – and the hemisphere really will be his.
View image in fullscreen Flávio Bolsonaro, centre, on the campaign trail in São Paulo last week. Photograph: Allison Sales/AP The White House has not simply been watching the election from afar. Since Trump returned to power in January 2025, administration officials and Maga-world allies have been doing what they can to damage Lula and boost the Bolsonaros. Initially, the aim of the support was to keep Jair Bolsonaro out of jail. Like Trump, he had not accepted defeat at the ballot box when he lost in the 2022 general election. Like Trump, his supporters stormed government buildings. But there were two crucial differences in Brazil – the seriousness of Bolsonaro’s attempt to hold on to power, and the determination of Brazilians that he should be held to account.
Investigators uncovered a sprawling conspiracy led by Bolsonaro and seven of his closest allies to keep him in power. It included an astonishing plot to kill Lula and his running mate, as well as a supreme court judge. A draft decree had been written that would overturn the result. The military would step in and ensure Bolosnaro returned to power. But the plot failed and Bolsonaro and allies, including his defence minister and the navy chief, were arrested and put on trial.
In response, Trump threatened in July 2025 to impose a 50% tariff on all imports from Brazil, arguing the case against Bolsonaro was a “witch hunt”. This blatant attempt at interfering in the judicial procedure of another country backfired. Lula made clear he wouldn’t bow to US pressure, the trial went ahead and Bolsonaro was found guilty and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Lula also received a bump in the polls after standing up to Trump.
In July, as the election campaign was kicking into gear, Trump tried his tariff trick again, imposing a new 25% rate on some Brazilian goods. The state department then tried to dispatch two officials to Brazil to investigate “electoral integrity” – Brazil denied them visas, accusing the officials of coming to “meddle in Brazil’s elections”.
In the final weeks of the campaign, Lula has leaned into those accusations. A recent advert accused Flávio Bolsonaro of being “Trump’s candidate” and said the US president wants “ to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust ”. What remains unclear is whether the White House’s strategy in Brazil is working. “Some in Brazil joke that Lula’s most effective surrogate is Trump,” Brian Winter, editor in chief of Americas Quarterly, told me.
Indeed, while Latin American countries have undoubtedly moved to the right in the past 18 months, US interference, despite Trump’s boasts, has arguably had little direct impact. In Peru and Chile, the Trump-aligned candidates were careful not to seek his endorsement for fear it would cause more trouble than it was worth. In Bolivia, the leftwing Mas government was responsible for its own downfall , winning just 3.16% in last year’s election after 20 years of increasingly chaotic rule.
3:43 How Trump is meddling in Brazil’s election – explainer The biggest reason countries have moved to the right has nothing to do with the US and everything to do with safety and security at home. Organised crime gangs, many of them linked to drug trafficking, are increasing in power. As Crisis Group put it in a report last year , while drug-related organised crime has been a problem across the continent for decades, “never has it spread so wide, and rarely has it penetrated so deeply into states and communities”. articles.title: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind
articles.description: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
articles.body:
‘AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying … jobs in the global economy. Women are just strikingly underrepresented.’ Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying … jobs in the global economy. Women are just strikingly underrepresented.’ Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images Reworked AI (artificial intelligence) The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
About this content Arielle Pardes Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T here’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI.
The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present.
“A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.”
Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.
Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared to 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recent report from LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’s research shows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI.
AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have.
“AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.”
The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said.
“What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs.
Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now hold about one-third of tech jobs in the US. But research has found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement.
Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.”
Putatunda said it’s not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up.
“If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.”
Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went on maternity leave for four months , and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare.
“That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.”
The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI.
“Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.”
When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women.

articles.title: The first step of caring for your makeup is storing it right. We asked experts how to
articles.description: Eyeing the new drop from your favorite brand? Make it go the extra mile with these expert tips
articles.body:
Photograph: EzumeImages/Getty Images/iStockphoto View image in fullscreen Photograph: EzumeImages/Getty Images/iStockphoto The Filter US Life and style The first step of caring for your makeup is storing it right. We asked experts how to Eyeing the new drop from your favorite brand? Make it go the extra mile with these expert tips
Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things
The best beauty advent calendars in the US in 2026 – tested and vetted
Lauren Gould Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Each week the Filter newsletter cuts through the noise to bring you smart, practical recommendations on how to live better – from what is worth buying to the tools, habits and ideas that actually last.
I hate throwing away my makeup. My beloved 2010s Naked eyeshadow palette and liquid matte lipsticks hung out in my white Ikea drawers well past their expiration dates.
So, while this week we recommended a plethora of beauty products – from Korean skincare to buzzy advent calendars – we want to help you actually use these items before they inevitably expire.
I asked three experts for their best advice on preserving the life of these items and reducing the chance that they end up in a landfill.
The best beauty advent calendars in the US in 2026 – tested and vetted
Inside Seoul’s K-beauty ‘mecca’: I hunted for the best skincare at the world’s biggest Korean beauty store
Keep a Sharpie in your makeup drawer Multiple experts I spoke to suggested labeling your items after opening, so that you know how long you have to use them before they expire.
Kim Chang, an aesthetician at Baylor University suggested storing a few permanent markers in your makeup drawer so that you can write the date you opened the item.
To keep track of how long you should be using your new lip gloss, check its PAO (period after opening). This is commonly found on the back of a product’s packaging. Look for a little icon of an open jar with a number next to it. That’s the number of months the product is good for after opening, said Dr Leyte Winfield , a chemist and director of Spelman’s Cosmetic Science Program .
View image in fullscreen Photograph: Lauren Gould/The Guardian Don’t store items in your bathroom “Many, like myself, store products in the bathroom for ease of access. Storing the item in a room other than the bathroom is recommended, while others may need to be refrigerated,” Winfield advised. You don’t need a fancy skincare fridge for your lotions and potions, but a decorative (and functional) basket or two would be a good place to start.
Avoid contamination Bacteria can decrease the longevity of your cosmetics, especially if you’re dipping into your moisturizer or lip gloss with your bare hands (or fingers).
Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to The Filter US
A guide to buying fewer, better products.
“Contaminants enter the product due to repeated application, even if an application tool is used,” said Winfield. Chang said you can opt for packaging that reduces the times you have to put your fingers into an item, like push-top moisturizers. (Also, wash your makeup brushes! )
Think before you buy With new beauty products entering the market every day, I am often tempted to grab the newest Rhode launch or viral skincare product. However, you can (and should) be intentional with your purchasing power. “I think it’s useful to consider shelf life at the point of purchase. If someone only uses a product occasionally, buying a very large size or opening several similar products at once may make it harder to use them within their recommended period,” said Yujiao Wang, who researched consumer attitudes on expired cosmetics.
And, if you need makeup for a special event, Chang advised getting it done professionally, rather than purchasing new items.
We have all had that one annoying purchase we’ve dragged our feet on for months – whether it’s a new set of bedsheets or a pan that doesn’t leave your eggs stuck to the bottom.
Have a current product you’re struggling to find or one you keep considering but can’t quite pull the trigger on? Email us at thefilter.us@theguardian.com. (While all responses will remain anonymous, we may use them in a future newsletter or story.)

articles.title: White House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirt
articles.description: Beni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House says
articles.body:
Donald Trump takes questions from members of the media, including Beni Rae Harmony, on Air Force One after a two-day visit to Ireland, on 13 September. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters View image in fullscreen Donald Trump takes questions from members of the media, including Beni Rae Harmony, on Air Force One after a two-day visit to Ireland, on 13 September. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters Trump administration White House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirt Beni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House says
Prefer the Guardian on Google The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle.
Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, revealed on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.
According to a LinkedIn profile , Harmony, 24, previously worked as a producer for the far-right Turning Point USA host Jack Posobiec – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida.
In 2021, when Gosar was censured by the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recorded an outraged defense of her boss for his YouTube channel.
The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by a far-right Republican House candidate, Jarome Bell, who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022.
A screenshot of that post, published by the Daily Mirror , shows that it included the caption: “My campaign Public Affairs Director @beniraeharmony is a beast. This is how we roll.”
Harmony appeared to verify the authenticity of the photograph in December 2021, when it was shared on social media by an anti-Maga outlet, PatriotTakes, which also identified her as an aide to Gosar.
The next day, Harmony replied to the PatriotTakes post of the image with another image of herself, wearing the same shirt in the same location and grinning into the camera. When another social media user posted a sarcastic question about the relationship between the older man and the young woman seen in the image, asking: “Daughter or date?”, Harmony replied with a one-word answer: “Uncle.”
Biden at the time was serving his lone term in the Oval Office, and Trump supporters chanting “Fuck Joe Biden” at a Nascar race that autumn inspired a viral meme featuring a variation of the slogan.
Harmony did not reply to requests to comment on the photograph. But the White House press office responded with a statement from a deputy press secretary, Anna Kelly, who praised the new hire for her advocacy of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, while ostensibly covering the president as a journalist.
“Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent,” Kelly wrote. “She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an Assistant Press Secretary – we look forward to having her on board!”
Harmony joins a White House press office that has taken unprecedented steps to ensure that the president is surrounded at all times by correspondents from partisan outlets who shower him with praise, and limit or deny access to reporters from nonpartisan outlets who challenge him.
Trump has tried to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House entirely, for what he considers overly negative coverage, and his aides now select which outlets are in place to ask him questions, with frequent slots reserved for correspondents who openly support him.
Harmony became the White House correspondent for Real America’s Voice after her predecessor, Brian Glenn, fell out of favor with Trump when his partner, Marjorie Taylor Greene, broke with the president and accused him of betraying the Maga movement.
Glenn had previously worked hard to advance Trump’s political agenda when invited by the president to ask questions. In 2025, for instance, Glenn pointedly asked Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, why he refused to wear a suit in the Oval Office, a question that inflamed an already volatile encounter.
During a press availability on Air Force One last month, Trump approached reporters with a sheaf of papers in his left hand. Harmony asked Trump a series of friendly questions that seemed designed to help him score political points. As TMZ reported on Friday, Associated Press photographs taken during that exchange showed that Harmony’s name was at the top of the first page in the president’s hand, suggesting that he might have been holding her résumé as he took her questions.
Harmony achieved a measure of celebrity in the rightwing media in 2025, when she left her job as an on-air host at a local TV station in Springfield, Illinois, after delivering an on-air tribute to the late Charlie Kirk, describing him as her first boss and mentor.
The station’s news director denied that Harmony had been suspended over the tribute, as she claimed, and clarified that she had never been a member of its news team, and instead hosted a program run by the channel’s sales department that featured clients who paid to be interviewed on television.

articles.title: Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
articles.description: Far-right challenger and son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro put in a stronger than expected showing, with Lula calling the result ‘unexpected’
articles.body:
2:54 Lula admits Brazil election result ‘unexpected’ as Bolsonaro leads first round – video Brazil Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula Far-right challenger and son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro put in a stronger than expected showing, with Lula calling the result ‘unexpected’
Prefer the Guardian on Google Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.
With 99.9% of votes counted, the 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president, Jair Bolsonaro, had won 47%, meaning he will now face a 25 October showdown with his 80-year-old rival. Lula received 45.1%. Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m.
Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite and is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, who included Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%.
Brazil’s far-right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, was elected to the lower house of congress. Bolsonaro’s former infrastructure minister, Tarcísio de Freitas, was reelected as governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s most populous and economically important state.
Of the 54 senators elected, 34 were from the right or far right.
Flávio Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital, Brasília, that the result signalled “the end of an era” for Lula’s Workers’ party. “Lula has fought seven presidential elections. He’s worried about power. I am worried about the future of Brazil,” he said.
​Speaking in Sāo Paulo, Lula put a brave face on a difficult night for the left. “We have just had a lesson in Brazilian democracy,” he said. “The result is often unexpected. We can never get everything we wanted. I confess to you that I was convinced I was going to win the election in the first round … But we have a second round.” Lula said Bolsonaro’s “dark past” would become clearer to voters in the lead-up to that vote. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil.”
View image in fullscreen Lula speaks to supporters following the partial results of the presidential election. Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty Images Earlier, as he cast this vote, Lula said Latin America’s largest democracy faced a stark choice, highlighting his adversary’s well-documented links to members of Rio’s underworld , including once employing close relatives of a notorious contract killer.
Lula, who became Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and was returned to office in 2006 and 2022, is hoping to secure a historic fourth non-consecutive term in this year’s election.
Allies of the veteran leftwinger called the election a crucial battle in the fight against a far-right movement that less than four years ago brought chaos to the capital, Brasília, during an unsuccessful attempt to overturn the result of the 2022 election, when Lula beat the incumbent president, Jair Bolsonaro.
View image in fullscreen Supporters of Flávio Bolsonaro react after the country’s electoral authority announced the runoff. Photograph: Tita Barros/Reuters Bolsonaro hopes winning the presidency will allow him to free his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after refusing to accept he had lost the last election to Lula. Ahead of the election he also called for tactical voting from conservatives who are not supporters of Bolsonarismo , but want to vote Lula out of power.
Read more As well as the president, Brazil’s nearly 159 million voters were choosing state parliamentarians, 27 state governors, 513 members of the lower house and 54 members of the 81-seat senate. Bolsonaro supporters made the senate race a priority because senators are the only lawmakers who can impeach supreme court justices – a demand among Bolsonaristas since the court jailed the former president for attempting a coup.
Hundreds of leftwingers had gathered at the heart of Laranjeiras, one of Rio’s most leftwing neighbourhoods, hoping to celebrate a Lula win to the sound of samba. But the mood soured and tears were shed as the hours passed and Bolsonaro’s lead over Lula held.
“It’s so sad that the Brazilian people … have opted for so much retrogression,” said Marcelo Mac, one of the owners of Miolo, a leftwing bar in Laranjeiras, as the scale of the rightwing advance was confirmed on Sunday night.
Mac, 46, voiced perplexity that the son of the man who tried to stage a coup only four years ago was now in pole position to become Brazil’s next leader. “He’s such an abominable guy that he manages to be even worse than his father,” Mac said of Bolsonaro.
Beside the bar a yellow flag stamped with Lula’s face carried the slogan: “Turn left”. But Brazil had voted for a turn to the far right.
View image in fullscreen A Lula supporter dressed as Our Lady of Aparecida at a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday. A row over the saint has caused a nationwide outcry – which could favour Lula, who is Catholic. Photograph: Pilar Olivares/Reuters Bolsonaro seemed to have the wind in his sails in the final days before Sunday’s vote, amid public frustration at a cost of living crisis and urban violence.
Read more But opinion polls failed to predict the scale of the rightwing triumph.
Shop assistant Italo Andrade dos Santos, ​a 31​-year-old Bolsonaro voter, had to keep his celebrations restrained behind the counter of the pharmacy where he was working a Sunday night shift. “I was a little di

articles.description: Brazilians have voted in a highly polarised presidential election between incumbent leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva -seeking a fourth presidential mandate - and right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who emerged as the leading figure of the conservative movement following the conviction and imprisonment of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro

articles.title: Brazil presidential election 2026: first-round live results
articles.description: Incumbent leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro. Follow the latest results live
articles.body:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of the presidential race
Brazil’s president is directly elected: each voter’s ballot counts equally and there is no electoral college. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the valid votes cast in the first round, a second runoff election will be held three weeks later between the two candidates who polled highest.
According to opinion polls, there are two leading candidates. The first is the incumbent president, Lula, 80, a veteran of the Brazilian left who has served three terms. During his first two terms, between 2003 and 2011, he was credited with overseeing a historic period of commodity-fuelled growth and poverty reduction.
Brazilian presidents are limited to two consecutive terms, so if he wins this time he will not be able to stand in 2030. In 2018 Lula was jailed on corruption charges, although his conviction was quashed after 580 days behind bars.
Lula’s principal opponent is the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison. Flávio is a 45-year-old lawyer and a former senator from Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election but has endorsed his son’s campaign and hopes to regain his freedom if he wins.
Opinion polls suggest no other candidate will come close to the two frontrunners, but neither is there a clear leader in polling for the 25 October runoff. The new leader will take power on 5 January 2027.
One of the most important states to watch is Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, and is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing in Minas. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate there by more than 1.7m votes and was elected president.
Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000 and also won the nationwide race. History suggests that whoever wins Minas, will win the election.

articles.title: Woman in Cornell rape allegations case targeted with threats, her lawyer says
articles.description: Attorney says people have threatened to silence or harm ‘Jane Doe’ if she does not withdraw civil lawsuit
articles.body:
Cornell University’s Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York. Photograph: Lauren Petracca/Reuters View image in fullscreen Cornell University’s Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York. Photograph: Lauren Petracca/Reuters US universities Woman in Cornell rape allegations case targeted with threats, her lawyer says Attorney says people have threatened to silence or harm ‘Jane Doe’ if she does not withdraw civil lawsuit
Prefer the Guardian on Google The woman who has alleged that ⁠ she was drugged ⁠and raped ​by Cornell University students has been the target of threats, her lawyer said on Sunday.
Read more Thomas Giuffra, who represents the ⁠woman identified as “Jane Doe”, told CNN that people have threatened to silence or harm her if she does not withdraw her civil lawsuit ⁠alleging that several members of a Cornell fraternity drugged and raped her in 2024.
“She’s ​received multiple threats,” Giuffra said on ‌CNN’s State of the Union.
Giuffra ‌said he had also been threatened.
“I’m not afraid of these people,” he ‌said. “But the threats, the abuse to protect what’s going on, the status quo – these guys are disgusting. They should stay in their mother’s basement and stay out of the world.“
The Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said in a video message on Saturday that the university will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on ‌campus after the outcry over the school’s handling of the rape allegations.
“At their best, these organizations can provide students with friendship, belonging, ​mentorship and a powerful sense of community,” he said. “But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility.”
Since the lawsuit was filed in September, prosecutors in Tompkins county, New York – where Cornell is – have been criticized for their initial handling of the allegations in 2024. ⁠The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, on Thursday named state attorney general ​Letitia James as special prosecutor ​to look into the case.
Donald Trump, a critic of James for years, lambasted ​the decision to ‌appoint her. “And I ​feel badly for whoever ​she’s looking at because they won’t get a fair shake,” the president told reporters on Friday.
Asked about Trump’s comment, Giuffra said the case shouldn’t be politicized. “It has nothing to do with politics,” Giuffra said.
Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: California woman arrested and accused of spying on Taiwan president’s son for China
articles.description: The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport before she left for China, the agency said
articles.body:
A California woman, Wanying Zhang, is arrested by the FBI at Los Angeles International airport after US authorities accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te at the behest of Chinese officials. Photograph: Bill Essayli/Reuters View image in fullscreen A California woman, Wanying Zhang, is arrested by the FBI at Los Angeles International airport after US authorities accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te at the behest of Chinese officials. Photograph: Bill Essayli/Reuters China California woman arrested and accused of spying on Taiwan president’s son for China The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport before she left for China, the agency said
Prefer the Guardian on Google US authorities arrested a California ⁠woman on ​Sunday, accusing her of spying on the son of Taiwan’s president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China , the agency said in a ⁠statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Read more Zhang surveilled a ​son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the ‌FBI alleged. The agency ‌did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report ‌identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident.
Taiwan’s presidential office described Zhang’s alleged actions as a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.
“Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
China’s foreign ministry did not respond to ‌a request for comment.
The Justice Department alleged Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and licence plate information of the Taiwanese president’s son and his family.
Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection ⁠and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, ​the first assistant US ​attorney for the Central District of ​California, alleged in a statement.
It was not immediately clear whether Zhang ​had a defence attorney. She ‌will appear on ​Monday in a ​Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said.
Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as ​Chinese territory. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.
Washington does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is the island’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.
